facts.text: In ancient India, a group of village settlements together formed a 'Janapada'.
facts.quote: A group of such villages together formed a 'Janapada'.

facts.text: Some Janapadas became powerful with armies, fertile lands, efficient governance and flourishing trade, evolving into 'Mahajanapadas'.
facts.quote: They possessed armies, fertile lands, efficient governance and flourishing trade. These Janapadas expanded in course of time evolving into 'Mahajanapadas'.

facts.text: The Post-Vedic Period is dated approximately from 1000 BCE to 600 BCE; permanent settlements of this time were called Janapadas.
facts.quote: Generally, the Post-Vedic Period is dated approximately from 1000 BCE to 600 BCE. During this period, gradually people had permanent settlements. These settlements came to be known as 'Janapadas'.

facts.text: A Janapada is a community of people living in a specific geographical region, engaged in agriculture, animal husbandry and trade.
facts.quote: A 'Janapada' is a community of people living in a specific geographical region. These people living together were engaged in agriculture, animal husbandry and trade.

facts.text: Janapadas were named after the respective tribe.
facts.quote: Since these communities belonged to certain tribe, the Janapadas were named after the respective tribe.

facts.text: Each Janapada had a chieftain, but most decisions were made with the elders; life was based on mutual cooperation.
facts.quote: Each Janapada had a chieftain. However, most of the decisions were made in consultation with the elders of the community. The way of life in a Janapada was based on mutual cooperation.

facts.text: The Janapada is considered the first of the ancient states in ancient India.
facts.quote: The Janapada is considered the first of the ancient states in ancient India, wherein importance was given to public participation, collective decision-making and social organization.

facts.text: Around the 6th century BCE, certain Janapadas became powerful kingdoms called Mahajanapadas, with villages, towns, trade routes and armed forces.
facts.quote: Around the 6th century BCE, certain Janapadas became powerful in terms of economic system, military organization and administration. These powerful kingdoms were called as 'Mahajanapadas'. The Mahajanapadas included many villages, towns, trade routes and had armed forces.

facts.text: A King or a Council of Advisors was at the head of the administration in Mahajanapadas.
facts.quote: A King or a Council of Advisors were at the head of the administration in Mahajanapadas.

facts.text: Some Janapadas expanded by conquering neighbours; by the 6th century BCE, sixteen Mahajanapadas had attained great importance.
facts.quote: Some Janapadas expanded by conquering the neighboring Janapadas and annexing their territories. By the 6th century BCE, sixteen Mahajanapadas had attained great importance.

facts.text: The development of the Mahajanapadas was an important stage before the emergence of empires.
facts.quote: The development of the Mahajanapadas was an important stage before the emergence of empires.

facts.text: Of the sixteen Mahajanapadas, Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti gradually became the most powerful.
facts.quote: Out of the sixteen Mahajanapadas, four of them, namely Magadha, Kosala, Vatsa and Avanti gradually became the most powerful.

facts.text: Mahajanapadas were larger in population, territory and resources than the Janapadas.
facts.quote: Mahajanapadas were larger in terms of population, territory and resources than the Janapadas.

facts.text: Mahajanapadas where common people took part in administration were called 'Ganarajya' (Republic); the king was not the absolute authority and an advisory council of elders, warriors or elected representatives assisted him.
facts.quote: These Mahajanapadas were known as 'Ganarajya' (Republic). In these republics, king was not the absolute authority. The King was assisted in decision-making by an advisory council. This council consisted of elders, warriors or elected representatives of the people.

facts.text: Members of the 'Ganaparishad' (Council of the Republic) were seniors of the community and made decisions together.
facts.quote: The members of the 'Ganaparishad' (Council of the Republic) were seniors of the community. The members of the Ganaparishad together made decisions regarding state administration.

facts.text: The assembly hall where these discussions took place was called the 'Santhagara'.
facts.quote: The assembly hall where these discussions took place was known as the 'Santhagara'.

facts.text: In the Republic of the Vrijjis common citizens took part in decisions; the Malla Republic had collective leadership; monarchy and oligarchy coexisted.
facts.quote: For instance, in the Republic of the Vrijjis common citizens actively participated in the decision-making process. Similarly, the Malla Republic also followed a system of collective leadership. ... in ancient India, monarchy and oligarchy coexisted.

facts.text: In the Gana parishad decisions were made by majority, using open vote, voice vote or secret vote.
facts.quote: In the Gana parishad, decisions were made by majority. Various methods were adopted to decide the majority, such as open vote, voice vote or secret vote.

facts.text: A member's vote was 'chhand'; coloured sticks called 'Shalaka' were the ballot; the 'Shalaka-grahaka' was in charge of voting; absent members could vote by proxy.
facts.quote: A member's vote was called 'chhand'. Coloured sticks called as 'Shalaka' were used as ballot. The person in-charge of the voting process was called 'Shalaka-grahaka'. An absent member was permitted to vote by proxy.

facts.text: Around the 6th century BCE, Magadha emerged as the most powerful and influential Mahajanapada.
facts.quote: Around 6th century BCE, Magadha emerged as the most powerful and influential Mahajanapada.

facts.text: Magadha's geographical advantage: fertile land along the River Ganges and use of waterways for trade.
facts.quote: Fertile land along the banks of the River Ganges ... Use of waterways for trade

facts.text: Magadha had large natural deposits of iron that helped advance agriculture and weaponry.
facts.quote: Large natural deposits of iron that helped to adopt advance techniques of agriculture and weaponry.

facts.text: Pataliputra was an important military, political and economic centre; from it, control of the whole Magadha region became easier.
facts.quote: The capital was established at Pataliputra, since it was an important military, political and economic centre. From Pataliputra, the administration and control of the entire Magadha region became much easier.

facts.text: Magadha became an important trade centre exporting textiles, spices and metals.
facts.quote: It became an important trade centre from where valuable commodities such as textiles, spices and metals were exported.

facts.text: Other Mahajanapadas were annexed to Magadha and matrimonial alliances were made for expansion.
facts.quote: Other Mahajanapadas were annexed to Magadha. Matrimonial alliances were established for expansion of the kingdom.

facts.text: Magadha was the first empire to be established in India.
facts.quote: Magadha was the first empire to be established in India.

facts.text: King Bimbisara laid the foundation of the Magadha Empire; trade flourished and he established the capital at Rajagriha.
facts.quote: King Bimbisara laid the foundation of the Magadha Empire. During his rule, Magadha's trade flourished. ... He established Magadha's capital at Rajagriha

facts.text: Ajatshatru, Bimbisara's son, succeeded him and conquered the Mahajanapadas of Vrijji and Kosala.
facts.quote: Ajatshatru, Bimbisara's son, succeeded him. Ajatshatru also adopted a policy of expanding the Magadha kingdom. Ajatshatru conquered Mahajanpadas of Vrijji and Kosala.

facts.text: Ajatshatru's 'Mahashilakantaka' was a massive machine that hurled stones to demolish the walls of enemy fortresses.
facts.quote: He created a device called 'Mahashilakantaka' a massive machine which hurles stones. It helped to demolish the walls of enemy fortresses.

facts.text: The 'Rathamusala' was a specialised chariot with spiked iron rods that ran into enemy troops.
facts.quote: He also designed a specialized chariot known as 'Rathamusala'. It was equipped with spiked iron rods. This chariot would run into troops of enemy, causing heavy casualties.

facts.text: Ajatshatru established a new capital at Pataliputra (present-day Patna in Bihar).
facts.quote: Ajatshatru established a new capital at Pataliputra (present-day Patna in Bihar).

facts.text: Ajatshatru became a follower of Gautama Buddha; after the Buddha's Mahaparinirvana, the First Buddhist Council was held at Rajagriha during his reign.
facts.quote: Ajatshatru became a follower of Gautama Buddha. After Gautama Buddha's Mahaparinirvana, the First Buddhist Council was held at Rajagriha during Ajatshatru's reign.

facts.text: Shishunaga, who came after Ajatshatru, conquered Avanti, Vatsa and Kosala.
facts.quote: Among the kings who succeeded Ajatshatru, Shishunaga was a significant figure. He conquered the kingdoms of Avanti, Vatsa and Kosala

facts.text: The Nanda dynasty came after the Shishunagas; Mahapadmananda, its famous king, brought many small kingdoms of Northern India under his rule.
facts.quote: The Nanda dynasty came to power after the Shishunagas. Mahapadmananda was the famous king of the Nanda dynasty. He expanded the Magadha Empire. He brought many small kingdoms of Northern India under his rule.

facts.text: The Nanda kings were known for military might, immense wealth and taxation system; Magadha became the most powerful kingdom in the Nanda period.
facts.quote: The Nanda kings were known for military might, immense wealth and taxation system. During Nanda period, Magadha emerged as the most powerful kingdom.

facts.text: Dhanananda, the last Nanda king, was very arrogant; his taxation caused unrest and the administration became corrupt.
facts.quote: The last king of the dynasty, Dhanananda, was very arrogant. The taxation introduced by him created unrest among his subjects. Also, the administrative structure became corrupt.

facts.text: Acharya Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya ended the Nanda regime and laid the foundation of the Mauryan Empire.
facts.quote: Ultimately, Acharya Chanakya and Chandragupta Maurya ended the Nanda regime and laid foundation of the Mauryan Empire.
